_readme: One entry per section (keyed by the section id in index.html). Each source is one video. 'videoId' is the YouTube id (the part after watch?v=). 'format': 'short' for YouTube Shorts. 'saltPct' drives the 'Calculate salt' button; leave it out for non-salt techniques. Method steps and key points take an optional 't' (seconds into the video) to show a timestamp button. Optional 'intro' is a short friendly line shown above the video. For recipe sections, set 'recipeLabel' on the section (e.g. 'quick pickle recipe') and 'cook' on each source (the name in the card header); 'tip' adds a 'Tip from <cook>' box.

sources.title: Fermentation vs. Pickling: What's the Difference?
sources.creator: Wendy the Food Scientist
sources.intro: Here's Wendy the Food Scientist to explain it in under a minute.
sources.summary: A 38-second explainer from a food scientist. Fermenting relies on bacteria already on the food to make lactic acid over days or weeks; pickling skips the microbes and adds vinegar, so it's ready in hours. Either way the food ends up below pH 4.6, where harmful bacteria can't grow.

points.text: Not all pickles are fermented, and not all fermented foods are pickles.
Lacto-fermentation: bacteria naturally present on the food turn its sugars into lactic acid over days to weeks, building complex flavour and probiotics that may benefit your gut.
Pickling: no fermentation, just vinegar added to make the food acidic. It tastes bright and fresh within a few hours.
Both methods bring the pH below 4.6, which stops harmful bacteria growing.

sources.fromDescription: her fermented dill pickles use a 2% salt brine, and her basic vinegar pickling brine is equal parts vinegar and water with 2 tbsp sugar and 1.5 tsp salt.
sources.compare: Matches the written sources. One thing worth adding: pH 4.6 is the line for harmful bacteria, but yeasts and moulds can still grow below it, so keep ferments under the brine (see The science).

sources.title: How to make pickles like a chef
sources.creator: Fallow
sources.summary: Fallow, a London restaurant, makes crinkle-cut, restaurant-style cucumber pickles. The cucumbers are salted first to draw out water, then covered in a sweet and sharp brine of sugar, white wine vinegar and water, spiced with turmeric and mustard seed, and left for at least two days.
ingredients: Turmeric and mustard seed, or other whole spices

method.text: Slice the cucumbers. Fallow use a crinkle-cut knife for the classic pickle look.
Sprinkle with salt and leave for 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, mix the pickling liquid: 1 part sugar, 3 parts white wine vinegar and 2 parts water.
Add turmeric and mustard seed, or try other spices for different flavours.
Rinse the cucumbers, pack them into a jar and pour over the pickling liquid.
Seal and leave for at least 2 days. The longer, the better.
Serve on burgers, as a garnish or as a snack.

sources.compare: This is a quick pickle: the jar isn't heat-processed, so keep it in the fridge. Half the liquid is vinegar, which gives a properly sharp pickle, and salting the slices first helps them stay crunchy.

sources.title: 2-day veggie pickle trick
sources.creator: Sivan's Kitchen
sources.summary: Sivan turns the leftover vegetables at the bottom of the fridge into crunchy pickles instead of throwing them away. Any mix of veg goes into a jar with salt, a splash of white vinegar and water, then sits on the counter for two days before moving to the fridge.
ingredients: Any vegetables you have, cut up. Sivan uses cabbage, cauliflower, cucumber, red pepper, jalapeños, celery, carrots, radishes and dill
2 tbsp kosher salt per 1 litre jar
About ½ cup (120 ml) white distilled vinegar per jar

method.text: Cut up whatever vegetables need using.
Wash them well.
Pack them tightly into clean jars, pressing down as you go. Recycled jars are fine.
Add 2 tbsp kosher salt and about ½ cup white vinegar to each 1 litre jar.
Top up with filtered water to the brim, seal tightly and give it a good shake.
Leave on the counter for 2 days, then move to the fridge to keep them cold and crisp.

sources.compare: This sits halfway between a quick pickle and a ferment: it uses less vinegar than a classic quick pickle, and two days at room temperature lets some fermentation get going. Keep every piece under the liquid, use a clean jar and move it to the fridge after the two days. Kosher salt varies a lot in weight, so weigh it if you can. The salt-only version is a ferment, so the Brine ferments advice applies.
sources.tip: For a salt-only version, skip the vinegar and add an extra ½ tbsp salt.

sources.title: Quick pickle cucumber
sources.creator: Andy Cooks
sources.summary: Andy's all-purpose quick pickle: equal parts vinegar and water with a spoonful each of salt and sugar, heated and poured over sliced cucumber with dill, chilli flakes and peppercorns. They're ready to eat as soon as they've cooled.
ingredients: Dill, chilli flakes and black peppercorns, or your own aromatics

method.text: Slice the cucumber.
Put it in a clean jar with the dill, peppercorns and chilli flakes.
Heat the vinegar, water, salt and sugar in a small pan until it simmers.
Pour the hot liquid over the cucumber.
Cover, leave to cool completely, then seal. They're ready to eat once cool.

sources.compare: A classic fridge pickle with a half-vinegar brine, which is about as sharp as quick pickles get. The jar isn't heat-processed, so keep it in the fridge and use clean utensils when you dip in.
sources.tip: The same liquid works for cauliflower, courgettes, radishes and even watermelon rind. The pickles keep in the fridge for up to six months.

sources.title: Quick pickle almost any vegetable with 2 ingredients
sources.creator: Bon Appétit
sources.summary: Chris Morocco's two-ingredient shortcut: thinly sliced vegetables tossed with a big pinch of salt and seasoned rice vinegar, which already contains sugar and salt. They're ready whenever you need them and keep for a few weeks.
ingredients: Seasoned rice vinegar (it already has sugar and salt in it)

method.text: Slice the vegetables thinly. Chris finds slicing quicker and easier than chopping.
Add a big pinch of salt and a good splash of seasoned rice vinegar.
Toss everything together.
Leave until you're ready to use them.

sources.compare: Less a jar pickle than a quick dressing: no water and no measuring. Seasoned rice vinegar is milder than white vinegar. Chris says they keep for a few weeks; store them covered in the fridge.
